transcript:
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
President Trump could be facing a busy month of campaigning for congressional candidates
ahead of the midterms.
This week, he's been to Texas and Oklahoma, tonight he travels to Mobile, Alabama, tomorrow
the president is slated to go to Ohio, and on Monday, Nebraska.
Some Republicans and competitive racists have broken with the president over his war with
Iran, policies blamed for higher inflation, and Trump's immigration policy.
The latest NPR/PBS News/Marist poll of registered voters reaffirms other national surveys suggesting
strong disapproval of President Trump's job performance.
West Virginia Republican Senator Shelley Moore Capito says White House officials are "acknowledging
the headwinds" but adds the GOP has a strategy.
One voter concern?
Surging diesel prices.
Colorado Public Radio's Ray Solomon reports 9 out of 10 school buses across the U.S. run
on diesel.
The soaring cost of diesel fuel is hitting school districts where it hurts right in the
transportation budget.
Nathan Reimer is transportation director in the Jefferson County School District near
Denver, Colorado.
"You know, I didn't budget for a war in Iran to affect my diesel prices."
But some school districts have alternative bus fleets that run on electricity or fuels
like propane, and they haven't been affected by high diesel costs.
Most of those districts got federal funding for these school buses from the 2021 infrastructure
law.
The Trump administration halted that program earlier this year, calling it "a disaster
of wasteful spending."
For NPR News, I'm Rae Solomon in Boulder, Colorado.
New York Attorney General Letitia James is promising transparency as her office conducts
a new investigation into allegations that members of Cornell University Fraternity House
gang-raped a woman two years ago.
"We will review the facts, gather evidence, interview witnesses, and if warranted, pursue
prosecutions."
But the state AG says she will not focus on the actions of Tompkins County District Attorney
Matthew Van Houten.
The Justice Department is appealing a federal judge's ruling that reinstated a court-appointed
U.S. attorney in Washington state.
The fight's the latest in the legal battle over Trump administration's efforts to install
interim U.S. attorneys.
Here's NPR's Ryan Lucas.
The federal court in the Western District of Washington appointed Roger Rogoff, U.S.
attorney, in July after President Trump failed to fill the post with a Senate-confirmed pick.
Less than an hour after Rogoff was sworn in, Trump fired him.
Rogoff then sued, arguing, among other things, that his firing violated the Constitution's
Appointments Clause.
On Thursday, a federal judge agreed, saying federal law authorizes courts to appoint someone
until the vacancy is filled.
The judge ordered that Rogoff be reinstated as U.S. attorney.
The Justice Department has appealed the ruling.
Ryan Lucas, NPR News, Washington.
You're listening to NPR News.
CBS Sports reports that it is formally parting ways with Tony Romo, who's been an NFL game
analyst with the network for nine years.
CBS says the decision was mutual.
Romo, previously a four-time Pro Bowl quarterback with the Dallas Cowboys, has been on leave
since his July arrest for operating a vehicle while intoxicated.
Last month, he pleaded no contest to the charge.
Defense Secretary Pete Exeth is facing backlash over the war, a decision to cut the senior
ranks of the military by 20%, and the decision to open an office of religious affairs.
Our department is, you might say, putting on the full armor of God, because while we
wage physical war, we all know the real battle is spiritual.
The Pentagon has said the new office will not compel religious participation.
Animals may have evolved up to 200 million years before they show up on the fossil record,
and PRS Ping Wong with more.
The oldest animal fossils are about 550 million years old.
Ross Anderson, a natural historian at Oxford University, says they're mostly shells and
skeletons.
Presumably, animals had a history before this, but because the animals then are soft and
squishy, it's actually really hard to get them preserved as fossils.
New analysis by Anderson and his colleagues suggests that animals came long before that
when much of the Earth was a ball of ice.
Looking at evidence from sites around the world, they calculated the maximum age for
the origin of animals back some 750 million years ago.
These were probably sponge-like critters that lived on the seafloor.
While this research doesn't prove animals existed that long ago, Anderson says it gives
them a direction in which to dig for evidence.
It's NPR.
